subject: English
topic: Paragraph Completion — Choosing the Best Sentence to Complete a Passage (W12 B1)

questions.stem: Passage 1: 'Education is the foundation upon which all progress rests. Without it, societies cannot develop the skilled workforce needed for economic growth, nor can citizens make informed democratic choices. Across history, civilisations that invested heavily in education rose to prominence, while those that neglected it declined. _______________.' Which sentence BEST completes this paragraph?

options.option_text: Therefore, building schools is more expensive than building hospitals.
It is therefore not surprising that nations which prioritise education consistently outperform those that do not.
Students, however, often find education boring and irrelevant.
Education systems in most countries face severe funding shortages.

questions.explanation: B is correct. The paragraph builds an argument: education → progress; civilisations that invested → rose; those that neglected → declined. The concluding sentence must logically follow this cause-effect pattern. B ('not surprising that nations prioritising education outperform') is the natural conclusion restating the argument in the present tense. Trap: A (schools vs hospitals) = an irrelevant comparison not introduced in the passage; C (students find it boring) = contradicts the passage's positive view of education; D (funding shortages) = introduces a new unconnected problem.

questions.stem: Passage 1 (continued): 'The quality of education, however, matters as much as access. A child who attends school but learns nothing has not truly received education. _______________, we must focus not merely on enrolment figures but on what students actually learn inside the classroom.'

options.option_text: In conclusion
For instance
As a result
Therefore

questions.explanation: D is correct. The blank introduces the logical consequence of the preceding argument (attending school without learning = not truly educated). 'Therefore' = for that reason; expressing a logical conclusion. 'We must focus on what students learn' follows BECAUSE school attendance alone is insufficient. Trap: 'In conclusion' = signals the very end of an essay (the paragraph is not ending here); 'For instance' = introduces an example (no example follows); 'As a result' = similar to 'therefore' but usually introduces an outcome that has already happened, whereas 'therefore' suits prescriptive statements ('we must').

questions.stem: Passage 1 (continued): 'Rote learning, while efficient for memorising facts, fails to develop critical thinking skills. _______________. In today's rapidly changing economy, adaptability and problem-solving matter far more than the ability to recall a formula.'

options.option_text: However, some experts believe rote memorisation helps in examinations.
Students who can only memorise are poorly equipped for the modern world.
Moreover, rote learning is widely practised across India.
In addition, most teachers prefer using textbooks over discussions.

questions.explanation: B is correct. The passage moves from 'rote learning fails to develop critical thinking' to 'critical thinking matters in today's economy.' The bridge sentence must connect these two ideas — B does this by explicitly stating the consequence for students who only memorise. Trap: A (experts defend rote learning) = contradicts the paragraph's argument; C (rote widely practised) = true but doesn't bridge to the next sentence about modern economy; D (teachers prefer textbooks) = introduces an unrelated subject (teacher preferences).

questions.stem: Passage 1 (continued): 'Private tuition has exploded in recent years, with families spending enormous sums on after-school coaching. This trend is partly a response to overcrowded classrooms and inadequate teacher training. _______________. The coaching industry profits while systemic problems in government schools remain unaddressed.'

options.option_text: Yet it also reflects a troubling displacement of responsibility from the state to the individual family.
Hence, private schools offer better education than government schools.
Furthermore, private tutors earn more than government school teachers.
However, some students prefer learning on their own without tuition.

questions.explanation: A is correct. The passage critiques the private tuition boom as a symptom of systemic failure. The final sentence ('coaching industry profits while systemic problems remain unaddressed') continues this critical tone. Sentence A ('troubling displacement of responsibility') logically bridges: the boom is not just a market phenomenon but a governance failure where the state offloads educational responsibility to families. Trap: B (private > government schools) = a comparison the passage doesn't make; C (tutor salaries) = irrelevant to the passage's argument; D (students prefer self-learning) = introduces a new unrelated idea.

questions.stem: Passage 1 (concluded): 'Ultimately, education reform requires long-term political will, not quick fixes. Governments must invest in teacher training, curriculum design and infrastructure simultaneously. _______________; without it, even the best-designed policies will crumble under poor implementation.'

options.option_text: Teacher quality, however, is the most debated topic in education
Above all, the quality of classroom teachers is the single most decisive variable
In contrast, private schools invest more in teacher salaries
Consequently, the government must reduce examinations

questions.explanation: B is correct. The paragraph argues for long-term investment and lists three simultaneous needs (teacher training, curriculum, infrastructure). The semi-colon in the final clause ('without it, even best policies crumble') suggests the blank must name a SINGLE crucial element — 'it' refers back to whatever is named in the blank. B ('teacher quality is the single most decisive variable') introduces that singular 'it'. Trap: A ('most debated topic') = adds a meta-comment about debate, not a substantive argument; C (private schools) = introduces a comparison not relevant to the passage's reform focus; D ('reduce examinations') = a non-sequitur.

questions.stem: Passage 2: 'Climate technology has advanced dramatically over the past decade. Solar energy costs have fallen by over 90%, making it competitive with fossil fuels in many markets. Wind turbines have grown in both size and efficiency. _______________. The challenge is no longer whether clean energy can work, but how quickly we can scale it globally.'

options.option_text: However, fossil fuels remain popular in developing nations.
Battery storage technology has also improved, addressing the intermittency problem.
Climate scientists have warned about rising sea levels for decades.
Governments are still subsidising coal and oil production.

questions.explanation: B is correct. The passage lists progress in clean energy technology: solar costs down, wind turbines improved. The blank continues this list of technological advances. B (battery storage improving, addressing intermittency) is a third technological advancement that logically continues the pattern. The concluding sentence ('challenge is now scaling, not feasibility') confirms the blank must present a positive technological development. Trap: A (fossil fuels popular) = contradicts the positive technological momentum; C (sea levels) = a climate impact topic, not technology advance; D (governments subsidising coal) = a policy concern, not a technological advance.

questions.stem: Passage 2 (continued): 'Despite this progress, the transition to clean energy faces powerful opposition. Fossil fuel industries employ millions and contribute enormous revenues to governments. _______________. Policymakers must therefore navigate between the urgency of climate action and the political costs of disruption.'

options.option_text: Regions dependent on coal mining face the prospect of economic devastation if the transition is poorly managed.
Renewable energy companies are rapidly expanding their workforce.
Scientists have confirmed that the Earth is warming faster than predicted.
Electric vehicles are becoming increasingly affordable for consumers.

questions.explanation: A is correct. The passage pivots to challenges: fossil fuel opposition due to employment and revenue. The concluding sentence ('policymakers must navigate between climate urgency and disruption costs') requires the blank to explain WHY there are political costs. A ('coal-dependent regions face devastation') directly explains the human cost that makes disruption politically difficult. Trap: B (renewable companies expanding workforce) = positive news that undermines the challenge framing; C (Earth warming faster) = a climate science finding, not relevant to political obstacles; D (electric vehicles affordable) = a positive consumer trend unrelated to the political challenge.

questions.stem: Passage 2 (continued): 'The idea of a 'just transition' has gained currency in climate policy discussions. It acknowledges that the shift to clean energy must not leave vulnerable workers and communities behind. _______________. Without justice, climate policy risks becoming a burden borne disproportionately by those least responsible for emissions.'

options.option_text: Just transition programs include retraining workers, investing in affected communities and creating new jobs in green sectors.
Nevertheless, climate activists often ignore the economic concerns of fossil fuel workers.
The United Nations has set a target of net-zero emissions by 2050.
Many economists argue that carbon taxes are the most efficient tool.

questions.explanation: A is correct. The paragraph defines 'just transition' (not leaving workers behind) and ends with the principle that justice is needed to prevent inequitable burden. The blank must explain HOW a just transition is implemented in practice. A lists concrete components of just transition programs, which connects the abstract principle to tangible policy. Trap: B (activists ignore workers) = contradicts the positive framing of just transition; C (UN 2050 target) = introduces an unrelated target; D (carbon taxes) = a different policy tool with no connection to worker justice.

questions.stem: Passage 2 (continued): 'International climate finance remains woefully inadequate. Developed nations pledged $100 billion per year to help developing countries by 2020 — a target they have consistently missed. _______________. This gap undermines trust in the global climate process and weakens commitments from developing nations.'

options.option_text: In fact, the actual flows have been significantly lower, and much of what has been provided came as loans rather than grants.
However, developing nations have made remarkable progress in renewable energy deployment.
Meanwhile, clean energy investors are finding new opportunities in emerging markets.
As a result, carbon capture technology is receiving increased funding.

questions.explanation: A is correct. The passage sets up the problem: pledge missed. The concluding sentence ('this gap undermines trust') requires the blank to define WHAT 'gap' refers to — specifically how inadequate the actual flows were. A specifies that flows were lower AND structured as loans not grants (compounding the inadequacy). This gives concrete content to 'this gap' in the next sentence. Trap: B (developing nations' progress) = changes subject entirely; C (investor opportunities) = a positive contrast that would undermine the 'inadequate' argument; D (carbon capture funding) = a non-sequitur.

questions.stem: Passage 2 (concluded): 'The coming decade will be decisive for the climate. Either the world accelerates the transition to clean energy with the seriousness the science demands, or it locks in temperature rises that will cause immeasurable suffering for generations. _______________.'

options.option_text: Climate technology patents are increasingly held by developed nations.
Most people remain unaware of the severity of the climate crisis.
The choice, ultimately, is not scientific but political — a test of whether governments will act in time.
Nevertheless, many scientists remain optimistic about carbon capture solutions.

questions.explanation: C is correct. The paragraph presents a binary choice (act now or suffer later) and frames it as an urgent crossroads. The concluding sentence must provide a strong closing statement. C ('the choice is ultimately political, not scientific') elevates the entire argument to its core insight — the science is clear; what's missing is political will. This resonates with the passage's opening ('long-term political will'). Trap: A (patents held by developed nations) = a new economic topic introduced mid-conclusion; B (public unaware) = relevant but weakens the urgency ('even if true, doesn't address the binary choice'); D (scientists optimistic) = undercuts the urgency with false reassurance.
